name: Text to SQL
title: Text to SQL
answer: Text to SQL is the task of translating a natural language question into a SQL query that runs against a real schema and returns the answer. It is how business users query data without an analyst in between. The work sits between a question and a database, and the query it produces has to be valid for the tables and columns that actually exist. A good system returns the right rows, not just a query that parses.

sections.body: Text to SQL is the task of translating a natural language question into a SQL query that runs against a real schema and returns the answer. It is how business users query data without an analyst in between. The work sits between a question and a database, and the query it produces has to be valid for the tables and columns that actually exist. A good system returns the right rows, not just a query that parses.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A text to SQL system needs three things: a language model, a connection to the database, and a description of the schema. The schema description is usually supplied as data definition language, sample rows, or a curated semantic layer that names tables and columns in business terms. Model Context Protocol servers are one common way to expose a database to a model, and this site tracks 263 of its 2526 active servers for SQL databases and warehouses. Execution happens against the live database, so the system also needs a way to run the query and return results.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The common pattern is schema retrieval followed by generation. The system selects the tables and columns likely to matter, puts their definitions in the prompt, and asks the model to write SQL. More reliable setups add a validation step that parses the query, checks it against the catalog, and runs it in a sandbox before returning anything. Accuracy is measured by execution, meaning whether the query runs and whether the result matches the expected answer, not by string similarity to a reference query. Hard cases include ambiguous column names, joins across many tables, and questions that need business definitions the schema does not carry.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: A generated query can read, and in some configurations write, real data, so permissions matter more than the model choice. The safe pattern is to run the model under a read only role with row and column limits, and to keep write access out of the loop entirely. Provenance matters too: teams need to know which schema version, which prompt, and which model produced a query that returned a number someone acted on. Query logs, schema snapshots, and the generated SQL should be retained together so a result can be reproduced or explained later. Where personal or regulated data is involved, the same access rules that apply to an analyst apply to the model.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward systems that check their own work: generate, execute, inspect the error or the result, and revise. Semantic layers and curated metric definitions are becoming the main lever on accuracy, because most failures come from the model not knowing what a column means rather than from SQL syntax. Benchmarks continue to push on realistic schemas with many tables and on questions that require reasoning about joins. The unresolved question is trust: how much of a warehouse should a model be allowed to touch, and who signs off when the answer is wrong.
